title: What is known about 1RB0LD_1RC1RA_1LD0RB_1LE1LA_1RF0RC_---1RE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LD_1RC1RA_1LD0RB_1LE1LA_1RF0RC_---1RE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to a parity question about one fixed integer sequence. Lean proves (kernel) that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if some epoch ends with an even number of 1 0 pairs (halts_iff), and (native_decide) that the first three epochs end odd, so a halt can come at the end of the fourth epoch at the earliest, after more than 1079,981 steps; its outcome depends on the parity of a term of the sequence with an index of 39,991 digits, which nobody can compute.

claims.title: The macro step
claims.text: From every phase start 0^∞ 1^a 0 0 (10)^K 1^(2j+1) C> 0^∞ the machine reaches the next phase start given by mstep, for all a, K, j, or halts exactly when a = 0 and K is even. The pieces (one sweep, the two phase ends, the reset, the halt) are runs proved for all values of the variables.

claims.title: Halting reduced to the macro machine
claims.text: The machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of mstep from (3, 0, 1) (reached after 18 steps) gets stuck.

claims.title: Halting reduced to a parity question
claims.text: Let seq be the orbit of the map g(K, j) = (j + 3⌊K/2⌋ + 1, 0) for even K and (j + 3⌊K/2⌋ + 3, 1) for odd K, from (0, 1). The walls are A₁ = 3 and Ai+1 = 2(j + 3⌊K/2⌋) + 7 where (K, j) = seq Ai, as long as K is odd. The machine halts iff some (seq Ai).K is even.

claims.title: The first two epochs
claims.text: The walls of epochs 2 and 3 are 25 and 227,097 (epochs 1 and 2 end with K = 7 and K = 75,697, both odd).

claims.title: The third epoch ends odd too
claims.text: (seq 227097).K, a number of 132,845 bits, is odd, so the machine survives the third epoch; if it halts, it is at the end of epoch 4 or later.

claims.title: How long that is
claims.text: With the exact step counts of the rules, epoch 2 ends after about 1010 steps and epoch 3 after about 1079,981 (py/macro.py epochs, 5 minutes of big-integer arithmetic); the fourth epoch has a wall of about 5.6·1039990 ones, so it takes more than 10^(10^39989) steps. The macro step and its step counts agree with the direct simulator for the first 18 phases (1.8 million steps) (py/macro.py check).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Probably halts, unimaginably late
claims.text: If the parity of K at the end of each epoch behaves like a fair coin, the machine halts at the end of epoch 4 with probability 1/2, of epoch 5 with probability 1/4, and so on: it halts with probability 1, but no one can compute when, nor prove it.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known: it halts iff (seq A).K is even for one of the walls A = A₄, A₅, …; A₄ has 39,991 digits, so even the next parity is out of reach of direct computation.

check: python3 holdouts/1RB0LD_1RC1RA_1LD0RB_1LE1LA_1RF0RC_---1RE/py/macro.py check 18     # macro step against the simulator
python3 holdouts/1RB0LD_1RC1RA_1LD0RB_1LE1LA_1RF0RC_---1RE/py/macro.py epochs       # walls and step counts of the first three epochs

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but we know exactly what the question is. The machine spends a wall of 1s one cell at a time while a counter K grows by half each time; when the wall is gone it halts if K is even, and otherwise turns the whole tape into a new, vastly longer wall. Lean proves that this is all it does. The first three walls (3, 25 and 227,097 cells) end with K odd; the fourth has 39,991 digits.

facts.text: Halting is proved equivalent to a parity at the end of an epoch.
Wall of 39,991 digits: its parity is out of reach.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497).
After 109 steps the tape spans 42,338 cells (3 left of the start, 30,298 right), with a density of 1s of 0.67.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: What the tape is made of
html: Watch the tape each time the head reaches a new cell on the right: it is always made of four parts. On the left a solid wall of a 1s, then two 0s, then K copies of 1 0 (the pairs), and finally a solid block of an odd number of 1s, with the head (state C) on the blank cell just after it:

sections.heading: One sweep
html: From the right end the head runs left through the block (D and A alternate, temporarily turning it into 1 0 1 0 …), eats the last two pairs, and runs back right restoring the block, now six cells longer (B and A, then E, F fill in). So one sweep turns (1 0)^(k+2) 1^(2j+1) into (1 0)^k 1^(2j+7), in exactly 8j + 14 steps (theorem inner). The sweeps of one phase repeat until 0 or 1 pair is left; the tape grows by about one cell per sweep, which gives the square-root growth.

sections.heading: Phases: K grows by half, the wall shrinks by one
html: When the pairs run out, the head walks into the wall and takes one 1 from it, and the block is reread as new pairs: K pairs become a block of about 3K ones, which becomes about 3K/2 new pairs. Exactly, with J = j + 3⌊K/2⌋:

end of phasewall a ≥ 1wall a = 0
K even (no pair left)(a−1, J+1, 0)halt (F reads a 0)
K odd (one pair left)(a−1, J+3, 1)reset: new wall of 2J+7 ones, (2J+7, 0, 1)

So inside an epoch the pair count follows K → about 3K/2, a Collatz-like map, and j just remembers whether the last K was odd. From blank tape the first phase start is (3, 0, 1) after 18 steps. The K values go 0, 2, 4, 7 (wall gone, odd: reset), then 0, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 31, 48, 74, 112, …: every epoch replays the same sequence from K = 0, and only its length, the wall, changes.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The only halting transition is F reading a 0, and it is reached exactly when the wall is used up and the phase ends with no pair left (K even). Otherwise the head runs off the left end of the wall and the whole tape fills up with 1s: a new wall about three times as long as the last K, so the next epoch lasts exponentially longer.

So the machine halts iff for some epoch the A-th term of one fixed sequence is even. Computing the term with an index of 39,991 digits is hopeless (the numbers would have more digits than there are atoms), and nothing is known that predicts the parity. If parities behave like coin flips, the machine halts with probability 1, but after more than 10^(10^39989) steps. This is the same kind of open problem as the Collatz-like “cryptids” of BB(6).

sections.heading: What is proved
html: In Lean (kernel), for all values: every piece of a phase (lean/Rules.lean, generated by py/gen_rules.py), the macro step and its halt (mstep_sound, mstep_halt), and the reduction halts_iff: HaltsFromBlank ↔ ∃ i A, epochs i = some A ∧ (seq A).1 % 2 = 0. The walls 25 and 227,097 are checked by the kernel; the parity at the end of epoch 3 by native_decide (lean/Epoch3.lean), giving halts_late: any halt comes at the end of epoch 4 or later.

summary: A wall of 1s is spent one cell per phase while K pairs grow like K → 3K/2; when the wall runs out the machine halts iff K is even, otherwise the whole tape becomes a new, much longer wall (walls 3, 25, 227097, then a 39,991-digit one): halting is proved equivalent to this parity question.
